en: May the Five-faced One protect you—he who, at the joyful assembly of the gods beginning with Brahmā, saw that as the Daughter of the Mountain was being kissed on the head by her delighted mother-in-law during the marriage of Śiva, the moon, thinking "his face has met my face," laughed; and seeing her face, his own face quickly became beautiful with a smile. (1)

Moreover, may the various glances of Lord Śiva—astonished at Pārvatī’s lotus-face, blossoming at her breasts, expanding at the region of her hips, and spreading wide again at her feet; glances that move in diverse ways across each limb like figures in a painting, and which pierced him as he was already struck by the arrows of the flower-bowed god of love—may those glances bestow auspiciousness upon you. (2)
At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager speaks:

"There exists today that King Śrī Narasiṃhadeva, the crest-jewel of Karṇāṭaka, whose lotus feet are set upon the crowns of the lordly diadems of the assembly of all haughty kings; [a king] by whom the armies of the protector of gods (Indra)—held back in various battles and terrified—were defeated, such that the earth trembled as it was torn apart by the throngs of dancing, fearsome headless trunks, and the mountains were made to wander. (3)

The poetry of that illustrious Kaviśekhara—whose hand, through the blazing flames of the majesty of his exerted arm, dispels all calamities; who acts as the preceptor illuminating the path to the attainment of all virtues; who is the crest-jewel upon the crown of the lineage of Dhīreśvara; and whose disposition is pure in its generosity—takes hold of my heart. (4)

Thus, by this [author], who is a new Bharata illuminating the entire specialized science of music; whose sprout-like hands are devoted to the pair of lotus-feet of the Destroyer of the Cities (Śiva); who is a neck-ornament for the eloquence that beautifies all languages and dialects; for whom the great festival of Mīmāṃsā dances within the throats of his disciples as they constantly taste the essence of Soma; the grandson of Rāmeśvara and the son of the venerable Dhīreśvara of pure fame.

I have been commanded by the preeminent teacher Jyotirīśvara—the crest-jewel of poets and the birthplace of the fluttering blossoms that roam upon the summit of the great lineage of the sacred teachings—to perform the farce titled *The Assembly of Rogues*, which he composed out of his own curiosity. And what has been thus commanded must certainly be borne upon my head by me, as dear as a garland of *mālatī* flowers.

For thus, his glories now triumph—honored for their boldness in the graceful movements of the stage of the world’s three realms—acting as camphor, as liquid nectar, as the smile of the lotus, as swans, as frost, as the Himalayas, as masses of hail, and as strings of pearls; they are like the clusters of rays from the cool-rayed moon. (5)

Moreover, by that crest-jewel of poets, who was skilled in the grace of generosity, which gods were not honored in heaven? How many lords of the twice-born were not fully satisfied? Or how many poets were not revered? And which supplicants were not made successful every single day? (6)
Therefore, having summoned my beloved, I shall descend to the musical performance.
(Looking toward the tiring-room) Noble lady, this way, please.
(Entering) Actress: (Translation of the stage directions and dialogue provided above.)
I am here today. May my noble sir command me; what service may be performed to please you? Sūtradhāra:
Noble lady, do you not even know?

The poet who, out of curiosity, swiftly composes four hundred verses adorned with poetic bonds, structures, and ornaments in a single day—he, the renowned treasury of the sixty-four arts upon the surface of the earth, the master Jyotirīśa, a veritable ocean of the tradition of music, reigns victorious. (7)
"The farce titled *The Assembly of Rogues* (*Dhūrtasamāgama*), composed by him, has begun to be performed; therefore, let some music appropriate for the drama be sung.
The Actress (with modesty): "May the noble sir command me. What is the predominant sentiment (*rasa*) in this composition, with reference to which I shall sing?"
Sūtradhāra:

Indeed, spring is resonant with the humming of bees intoxicated by the thick fragrance of the nectar of full-blown *mālatī* flowers; it is a season where the erotic passion of the God of Love (*Anaṅga*) is perpetually unfolding. For thus it is:

With bees buzzing in the groves of blossoming *mallī* jasmine, with pollen emerging from rows of flowering mango trees, and with the auspicious beauty overflowing from the throats of joyful cuckoos—this very spring steals away the mind even of a sage. (8)
Naṭī:

The mango grove is stirred by breezes laden with pollen; its sweet warbling is taken up by the cuckoos; the bees are intoxicated by the nectar; and the faces of all the quarters have been made fragrant. (9)
This month of spring brings the hearts of the caravan of sages, who are supported by self-restraint, under the sway of passion, having uprooted their heavy fortitude. (10)
With staff and water-pot adorning his hands, his head graced by a most graceful sectarian mark, this walking embodiment of greed approaches, his beauty enhanced by the fluttering saffron robe. (11)
Noble lady, who is this person seen here and there, looking about like a rogue, wearing a garment of reddish-brown cloth that is slipping down, and carrying a staff and a bundle?
Sūtradhāra:
Noble lady!

He who is heard of from the mouths of people as one possessed of horses and chariots, devoid of the dharma of proper conduct, and a dandy among courtesans—who, though marked by long, upright sectarian marks, a water-pot, and a staff, is said to nourish a fierce hypocrisy throughout the entire city. (12)
Therefore, his very sight must be avoided from afar.
(Exeunt both. Thus ends the prologue.
(Then enters Viśvanagara, as described, followed by a Snātaka.
Viśvanagara [with world-weariness]:

I constantly meditate upon that noble Madhumathana—the Lord of the three worlds, who is without qualities (*nirguṇa*), beyond phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and the one who is meditated upon by yogis within the center of the heart-lotus; he whom I, the undecaying and primordial, know solely through pure consciousness (*jñāna*). (13)
The Snātaka (looking from the hermitage, to himself):

Oh, how delightful is the beauty of spring! For the bees, skilled in the essence of the nectar of blossoming flowers, intoxicated by love and enamored of the forest groves, drink in with passion the sweet, natural fragrance. And the cuckoos, crying out as they flutter about, steal away the consciousness of amorous women separated from their lovers—the very fame of the *jhankāra* sound of their jeweled girdles. (14)

O brother, those breezes from the sandalwood forests—which carry the fragrance of camphor, stir the beauty of the lotus groves, and cause the branches to tremble by their very nature; which bring delight to the world and display the pride of amorous play with the women of the gods; and which delude the three worlds—those breezes are cool and wafting the pollen of the Malaya mountains. (15)
"How then am I to endure this unbearable spring season with my single body? (She acts out her despondency.
Viśvanagara (gazing at the Snātaka):
Ah, you of evil conduct! Why do you appear so different today, with your neck bowed under the weight of anxiety? For instance:

There is heaviness in your sighs, emaciation of the body, vacuity upon the casting of a glance, a yellowish hue upon the moon of your face, faltering in your gait, and despondency in your heart; yet no movement at all is observed in you, for you have assumed a form exceedingly distressed. Therefore, I think that the five-arrowed god (Kāma) obscures your former nature and your steadfastness.
The Snātaka (standing with his face cast down in shame): "Venerable sir, this is indeed most embarrassing; therefore, it is not proper for me to appear before you.
Viśvanagara:
"There is no fault in describing one's own nature; let it be told. The Snātaka (affectionately):

"Venerable sir, today, on the banks of the city lotus-pool at Mahāprabhāda, I beheld a courtesan named Anaṅgasenā, whose beauty surpassed that of the city of the gods. From that moment onward, I see nothing but her everywhere."
Viśvanagara (clapping his hands and laughing loudly):
My dear boy! Today I too saw that very woman named Suratapriyā, who was fasting for a month. Pursuing her, I too have been pierced by the arrow of love that strikes the vital organs. For instance:

As if painted in the sky, as if inlaid in the quarters of the horizon, as if strewn everywhere, as if reflected in the lashes of my eyes, as if clinging to my mind, and as if bound within it—that beloved, the dwelling-place for the abode of lovely amorous sports, like a female bee upon the lotus of my heart, is so utterly overwhelmed by her intense passion that it is not known where she is. (17)
(Looking upward) My child! The divine thousand-rayed sun has ascended to midday. For thus it is:

the circle of the quarters is swallowed by mirages, the sky is streaked with the shadows of the sun’s rays, and the dust of the earth consists almost entirely of sparks from glowing embers. Travelers lie within the bowers of trees and creepers crowded with ponds, while the reservoirs of water, their waters reddened by the drinking of elephants, are agitated. (18)
(As they both walk about.
Mṛtāṅgāra:
"Venerable sir, to the north of our dwelling lives a woman who observes a month-long fast, named Suratapriyā. Let us go there. (Having said this, he walks away quickly.)
Viśvanagara:
If that is so, then our very desire has been fulfilled. Come, let us go right there. (They both walk about.
Snātaka (looking ahead and smelling a fragrance):

O noble sir, look, look! Here is the dwelling of some very wealthy man, which is seen from afar: its courtyard is adorned with pillars that resemble the heads of young elephants shorn by the Blessed One; it is beautified by young calves wandering here and there; and the vicinity of the residence is lovely with groups of women moving slowly, languidly stumbling due to the weight of their full, high breasts. O citizens, whose dwelling is this? (He recites this. [From behind the scenes:]

Before him shines this hermitage belonging to he who is renowned on earth by an ungraspable name—one whose every enjoyment was interrupted by the taste of the transformation of Fortune (Lakṣmī), and who, with his wealth constantly scattered, slept soundly with all anxiety dispelled. (19)
The Snātaka (having gone forward again):
Ho, ho, citizens! To whom does this residence belong? (Thus he recites again [the verse beginning with] "Lakṣmī" and so forth from behind the scenes. Viśvanagara:

"Ah! Why this persistence of yours in mentioning his name? Or rather, let it be as it may; listen. This is the hermitage of Mṛtāṅgāra Ṭhakkura. Child, enough of delay; let us enter the dwelling. (Having thus gesticulated entering the residence, they stand aside. (Then enters Mṛtāṅgāra, dressed in a state of dejection. Mṛtāṅgāra:—
This Kuvera, though disposed to spend, may well fall into poverty; yet even their very lives must be given by the wealthy to those who ask, not merely wealth. (20)
The Graduate (approaching):
O great Brahmin! The venerable citizens of Viśvanagara desire to partake of alms at your house.
Mṛtāṅgāra (to himself):

"Alas, what ill fortune is ours! That this comet has fallen upon me alone, leaving behind all these people of the city and its outskirts. What remedy can there be for this today? (Reflecting thus, he then says aloud with humility: "It is only fitting that sinless men like you should wander for alms at the house of one who, by virtue of serving the form of the Imperishable Lord, would be blessed and a sanctified abode. However, the Brahmin woman next door is attached to her brother, and the female messenger is pregnant; because of these births and deaths (*sūtaka*), you must go to another place. (21)
Viśvanagara (to himself):

Oh, what a deceitful practice this wicked man employs! Very well then; I shall awaken him. (Aloud) Long-lived one! How could there be the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*) for us, who are masters? And so says the *Smṛti*:
"Neither the wind by the fault of touch, nor fire by its act of burning, nor water by urine and excrement, nor a wandering mendicant (*maskarī*) by the fault of food. (22)
Mṛtāṅgāra (humbly): Holy sir! Even if it be so, it is nonetheless impossible. Behold:
due to drought, agriculture is ruined; due to the collapse of the kingdom, there is debt and the like; trade yields but little profit—what then can be said of one's morning meal? (23)
The Graduate (with anger, resorting to Sanskrit):
The Graduate (approaching)—
Fie upon the folly of Śrī, the daughter of the ocean!

She does not recognize one who is of noble birth, endowed with supreme virtues, possessed of integrity, righteous, devoted to right conduct, skilled in action, or adorned by progeny; rather, she serves one who is base, cruel, and devoid of a compassionate heart—for that reason, you have been chosen as her consort by Lakṣmī, the daughter of the ocean, who acts according to her own nature.

"O wretched Brahmins who have lost sight of the next world! At such an unbearable midday heat, why did you first beg for great wealth from Anada and then go to us to ask for alms? We must seek our own food.
Mṛtāṅgāra:
"Venerable sir, there lives in the house to the north of ours a woman named Suratapriyā, who observes a month-long fast. You should go there. (Having said this, he quickly walks away.)
Viśvanagara:
If that is so, then our very desire has been fulfilled. Come, let us go right there. (They both walk about.
Snātaka (looking ahead and smelling a fragrance):

"Sir, look, look! This woman, whose body is adorned with a single mark, frequents the temple of Agni, which exudes the fragrance of a great heap of incense. Therefore, this indeed is the bedchamber of Suratapriyā. Viśvanagara:
"It is said that she is truly clever, being one who fasts for a month. Come, let us approach. (They stand aside. Then Suratapriyā enters.
Suratapriyā:

The Dharma is not desired by me, for it involves much suffering; my true happiness lies in liberation. Wealth is fully capable of accomplishing everything, being the treasury of all the arts of the bodiless god of love. (25)
The Snātaka (approaching): Noble lady, your brother-in-law has arrived, eager for diversion. Suratapriyā (walking about and looking around):
Therefore, I approach you. (Approaching) Venerable sir, I bow to you.
Viśvanagara (with joy):
May you become the vessel for my desires.
Suratapriyā:
"Venerable sir, it is by your grace.
Viśvanagara:
"May it be so without delay.
Suratapriyā:
"Let the Blessed One command what must be done by me and what must be given."
Viśvanagara:
"O auspicious lady, what is there that we cannot give to you? For now, let there be alms alone.
Suratapriyā:
"Venerable sir, what kind of alms do you seek, at what time, and how many are your followers?
Viśvanagara (joyfully): "Listen."

Meat, black gram, paṭola, buttermilk, *baḍikā*, and *vāstūka* greens; the banyan tree is a source of *sañjīvanī*; furthermore, there is an abundance of varieties of fish and split mung beans; and most deliciously, milk, ghee, fresh curd, plantain fruit, and sugar—in short, O fair-faced one, let my alms be prepared quickly. (26)
Suratapriyā (smiling, to herself): Ah, by the grace of the best of gods, this great soul has become worthy of not being dismissed [by me]. (Aloud, joining her palms in reverence:

This body is joined with separation, and likewise my life-breaths have as their sole essence the fruit of righteousness (*dharma*). O you of noble fame, everything is dependent upon you; what external objects could there be that are of any real value? (27)
"Having entered the interior of the house, let the venerable one rest. As for me, however, I shall go about seeking alms.
The Snātaka (with derision): "Venerable sir, look, look! (Resorting to Sanskrit:)

Her tresses are withered, both her cheeks are sunken from side-long glances, the orb of her breasts has fallen, and the region of her hips is parched. Alas, alas! With her sidelong glances, smiles, and speech, she stages a festival for the eyes; what shall we say, or what can we do—is this some wicked, aged female ascetic? (28)
Viśvanagara:
Fie on you, fool! Why do you prattle like one fit for the company of the wicked? (To Suratapriyā: O auspicious lady! Go toward the kitchen; we too shall be coming shortly.
Suratapriyā:
"As the venerable one commands. (She exits.
Snātaka:
Venerable sir! May you remain right here until the alms are prepared. As for me, I shall return quickly once I have learned the news of Anaṅgasenā.
Viśvanagara:
My dear child, Haira, you may go now. (Thus they both walk about.
Snātaka:
"Sir! I have heard that Anaṅgasenā’s residence is located near the house of Mūlanāśana. Therefore, let us follow her very path.
Viśvanagara: "Then come, let us go before her; let us approach her. (They stand aside. Then Anaṅgasenā enters.)

The Snātaka (approaching suddenly): O venerable one! Behold, behold the beauty of Anaṅgasenā! Her eyes are as lovely as blue lotus petals; her face is like the full moon; her body is slender and curved by the weight of her high breasts; she walks with the slow gait of an elephant in rut; this young girl, radiant with loveliness, is surely the enchanting garland of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], the very life of the erotic sentiment. (29)
Viśvanagara (to himself):

That slender-limbed girl, whose lotus-face smiles with the flickering grace of collyrium for her eyes, who is the abode of intentional arts and dalliance, and who experiences horripilation at the sight of me—having observed my bodily gestures, she likely conceals the amorous arrangement established upon her body. (30)
(Aloud) You have observed correctly. For indeed:

her sacred bathing water is the nectar from her lotus-face; her eyes are two fresh blue lotuses; her row of teeth and nails are a heap of unbroken rice grains; the line of hair on her body is dūrvā grass; her pair of lofty breasts are a pair of fruits; and her lotus-hand is a leaf. I believe that she, her mind intent upon the worship of Madana, has offered these parts of her own body as sacrificial oblations. (31)
(Referring to Anaṅgasenā:

That penance which was performed in the past, the pilgrimages undertaken every day, and how my mind was rendered fulfilled through the abundant worship of Puruṣottama—the fruit of those actions has now been obtained, producing supreme joy. What then is the use of the flavor of scriptural discourses, or indeed of heaven or liberation? (32)

(Thus he gesticulates the state of his body. The Graduate (joyfully, to himself): Here is this lecher, who has approached me like a snake that has emerged from a mouse-hole. Very well; I shall ward him off with words preeminent in logic. (Aloud) Venerable sir, you who have transcended the sorrows of saṃsāra through equanimity and are solely intent upon liberation—how can you, having cast yourself into such a passion for love as this, which is like a bath in excrement, destroy yourself? Desist from this attachment to this wicked courtesan!
Viśvanagara (to himself):
My dear boy, do you not see that as long as the fickle glances of the deer-eyed women do not dance about, so long does discernment find a place in the hearts of the wise? (33)
Anaṅgasenā (smiling):
"Venerable sir, this person is indeed dependent on wealth; you are mocking yourself by acting as if you were weeping in a forest.
Viśvanagara:—
"How can there be an abundance of wealth for us who are renunciants? Therefore, let this body of mine be employed as you please.

(With affection) O girl with arms as tender as lotus petals, O fierce one with a formidable face, cast your glance upon me! This wretched ascetic, whose heart is drawn by the lotus of your countenance, is instantly sinking into the ocean of passion. (34)
The Snātaka: "O Blessed One! You who have transcended the sorrows of saṃsāra... (and so forth he recites).
Anaṅgasenā (resorting to Sanskrit):

O Blessed One, enough with this excessive deliberation! Having set aside the meaning of words, those free from envy meditate upon the path to liberation; they are impartial toward all, whether high-born, low-born, peaceful, or arrogant. With minds refined by equanimity toward passion and hatred, they dwell eternally like courtesans, gods, and mendicants—alas, why indeed does he sink into the ocean of desire? (35)
Viśvanagara:
"My dear, take my body! (He grasps her by the hem of her garment. Snātaka (approaching suddenly):
"You wretched wandering mendicant, you who have lost the next world! This girl was first in our possession as your son's bride; therefore, release her!
Viśvanagara:
"Fie, fool! She is our daughter-in-law, the wife of your guru, and equal to a mother. Why then do you pursue her?"
The Snātaka (angrily):
You lecherous wretches! As you speak thus, I shall make your shaven heads burst like overripe *mālūra* fruits with a blow of my staff! (Thus they quarrel with one another.
Anaṅgasenā (to herself):
"How was it placed in the hands of a rogue? Let it be so for now. (Aloud) "O noble sir! In such a great dispute as this of yours, let the venerable Asajjāya be made the authority. (He shows the knot.
Viśvanagara:
"Enough with showing the knot! Come, let us go right there. (All exit.)
Thus ends the first act-transition. (Then enter Asajjātimiśra and the Vidūṣaka.
Asajjātimiśra (with joy):
The enjoyment of the three worlds is the most excellent, yet even more so than that is the festival of sexual union; whether there be food or not, life cannot exist without sexual union. (1)
Child, you who deceive your kinsmen, come and study!
Vidūṣaka: As you command.

That which is a dream of a beautiful woman’s face, the gazing of an eye with languid lashes, or even that bodily contact on the pleasure-ground involving the pressing of her jar-like breasts and the graceful bending of arms—make this the essence of worldly existence, cultivated in your own heart as the sole state free from conceptual construction. What need have you for the burden of the patched rags of the intellect of the simple-minded, which is merely boiled over by disputation? (2)
Vidūṣaka:
Oh friend, even more than the enjoyment of another's wife, that very wealth which is stolen after breaking into another’s house is the essence of the three worlds! Look, look!

What is the use of trade, having caused the destruction of one's own wealth? Or what is the use of agriculture, which yields its fruit only through the labor of cattle, seed, and manure? What is the fruit of learning, when it is agitated by anxieties equal to death? Only the theft of another's wealth and the pleasure of gambling are the essence of the world. (3)
Thus, in this city of Dhūrtapura, I have become a disciple exactly like my teacher—you!
Asajjātimitra:

Oh, the life free from worldly motives for Vedic scholars like us in this city! For eight days now, there has been no one who speaks with integrity, no acquisition of gifts through fraudulent *śrāddha* rites, and no conversation with courtesans.
[Offstage]— Let it be announced to the honorable gentleman that two litigants stand at the door to have their case adjudicated.
Asajjātimiśra:
"My child, you deceiver of kinsmen, let the two disputants enter.
(The Vidūṣaka exits and re-enters with Viśvanagara, Snātaka, Anaṅgasenā, and others.
[Asajjāti] (observing Viśvanagara and Snātaka, to himself):
How has this unintended consequence arisen? (Aloud) Venerable sir, we are but guests; therefore, this is not the occasion for alms here.
Vidūṣaka:
O sir, these very people are the disputants. Let the sir adjudicate their dispute.
Asajjātimiśra: (With joy and respect) — Let a seat be brought for the Blessed One and for the Snātaka.
(The Vidūṣaka does so and seats them all.)
Mixed with those who are not fit for the assembly—
what is the plaintiff, and what is the defendant?
The *snātaka*—
"I am here, O Blessed One, with my own hand.
Asajjātimiśra:
"For those who speak according to logic, first there is the collection [of evidence], and afterwards the speech in response."
Viśvanagara:
This bundle is our ascetic staff.
Snātaka: [He takes it.]
"Let this Indrāsana-kollia of mine be bestowed upon the performance of the play.
Asajjātimiśra (taking it with respect, smelling it with delight):
"It shall be employed for something."

It induces sleep, is a cause for destroying the bodily humors, stimulates hunger, and expands the intellect; this food of Indra, which accords with the power of desire, has now been obtained by me through the force of destiny. (4)
Viśvanagara:
She who possesses independent youth and beautiful eyebrows is worthy of honor by all lovers; she has been seized by us, therefore she is my beloved. (5)
Asajjātimiśraḥ (writing on the ground in the vernacular, addressing the Snātaka): "Snātaka, give a prompt reply.
The Snātaka:
"She was previously seen by me; having given ten coins, she was brought here. Now that she has been obtained, she is dear to me. (6)
Asajjātimiśra:
Write back. Vidūṣaka: [writes].
O friends! Look, look! At the beauty of Anaṅgasenā!

Her face flashes like the orb of the moon; her eyes are a treasury for the playful flickering of blue lotuses; she is burdened by the weight of her breasts and slender-waisted, resembling the crescent of the new moon. (7)
A mixture of the unreal and the real:
"Oh, what exquisite skill in creation belongs to the Creator!

For thus—she whose eyes are as lovely as a shimmering blue wagtail, whose face possesses the beauty of the full autumnal moon, and whose divine form enchants the three worlds—this young maiden shines in the world like the fame of the steadfast Kāma. (8)

"O disputants! Let this Anaṅgasenā, who is the subject of this debate, be placed in the position of an umpire for as long as there is victory or defeat. And in such a state of impartiality, we ourselves, established by the King, shall serve as the umpires.
(Having brought Anaṅgasenā and seated her near him, and placing her hand upon his heart, with great joy:)

This hand of hers possesses the beauty of the calyx of a blooming lotus; it is cool, born from the moonstone produced by the rays of the moon; and being auspicious with the fragrance of musk and camphor, this delicate hand removes the fever of love. (9)
(Reflecting for a moment, then laughing loudly) O two disputants! This dispute of yours in the field of this kingdom is like that of two serpents. For it is thus:

"This fortunate woman is not yours; she does not belong even to you. She dwells in my presence; she is mine. Since she first engaged in play with me even in a dream, for that very reason she is indeed dear to me. (10)
Vidūṣaka (looking at Anaṅgasenā, aside):
O beautiful one! This gentleman here is a Buddha, a venerable naked ascetic, a wish-granting gem. Therefore, avoiding association with these people, let your youth bear fruit through union with me.
(He reveals himself.)
Anaṅgasenā (smiling): This has become a mockery of the assembly of rogues. Viśvanagara (with world-weariness):

"My dear Durācāra, a leech does not attach itself to the body of another leech. This plan of Mūlanāśaka is for the very purpose of uprooting us. So come, let us go to the house of Suratapriyā herself. (They both exit. Then enters Mūlanāśaka with a sudden entrance.
Mūlanāśaka:

Hey there! Anaṅgasenā, you know that as soon as I set out, you sent me to endure the pain of being bitten by Kāmadeva at every step. So give me back [the money] now; otherwise, I shall have to show you the king's fines.
Anaṅgasenā:
My dear friend, I shall give this very moment to you from my own person; therefore, be at ease.
Vidūṣaka: —
Who is this one of wicked appearance, wicked conduct, and wicked dress?
Asajjāti-miśra: Is he beyond the reach of the Blessed One? Look!

With his lips and nose cut off, his neck swollen with a goiter, his left eye blind, one hand fallen away, and his right foot afflicted with elephantiasis—indeed, that barber was utterly ruined at the root.
(The Root-Destroyer suddenly approaches and shows a mirror to everyone with great ceremony.
Asajjātimiśra:
Root-Destroyer! Let us have our nails and hair trimmed.
The destroyer of the root—
first, experience the sensation.
Mixed with the unarisen.
"Root-destroyer, for what purpose?
A root-destroyer—
oh, if you were to kill me first while I am still struggling, then why would I have to endure this agony?"
"Asajjātimiśra: Enough with the joking! Accept this reward.

(Having pulled Gañjākinī from the weaver, he gives it to him. Mūlanāśaka takes it respectfully, smells it with joy, uses a small portion, binds the hands and feet of Miśra, and acts out the act of execution.)

Mixed with unbearable pain—this heart breaks, the mind falls into delusion, and the joints of the bones in my entire body burst apart. Desist, desist from this craft! O root-destroyer, alas, alas, alas! Life itself seems to be cracking instantly. (12)
The Destroyer of the Root (shaking him): What? Is the son-in-law of the King of Magadha here? I shall slip away very quietly. (He exits.
Vidūṣaka (releasing the binding of the King's hands and feet):
"Sir, please command me; I shall accomplish whatever else you desire. Asajjātimisra (regaining consciousness):

"The entire kingdom has been enjoyed through deceit; this beloved wife has been obtained by fraudulent means; and you, humble and submissive, have become my disciple. There is nothing more dear to us in this world than this. (13)
Nevertheless, let this be:

may the clouds rain continuously at the proper time; may the earth be abundant with crops; may the rulers of men be devoted to the protection of their own dharma; may the Brahmins be filled with the three Vedas; may the cows, their udders bowed down by sweet milk, be free from calamity every day; and may virtuous people, intent on peace, be endowed with goodness. (14)
(Thus they all exit.
Thus ends the farce named *The Assembly of Rogues*, composed by the preeminent poet and teacher Jyotirīśvara.
